name: Karl Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to tech firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential, and your name won't go on anything.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right. I don't know what use my opinion is, but go on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Long Acre, Mr Dorran's place, about a hundred and twenty beef cattle being fattened and eighty acres of potatoes, plus some wheat. In winter I'm bedding the cattle with straw, feeding, and then in the potato store grading spuds on the old belt for most of the day. In spring and autumn I'm on the tractor, the old blue one, planting or carting the harvest. I've been there four years and I still get told off for driving too close to the hedges.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's hard about it right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Last winter potato prices were terrible, so Mr Dorran cut me from five days to four for three months. That hurt, because I'm already on low money and we were behind on the electric. My partner Leila works at the supermarket in town, shelves and the tills, and her wages kept us going. We've got maybe a week or two in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So nothing much changes. Fine by me. I don't use any of that AI stuff anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave things as they are. At the pub I'd say I never trusted all that talk. I don't go online much, so I'd just say it to whoever's at the bar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my worry isn't AI, it's potatoes. If prices crash again, Mr Dorran cuts my days again, and there's nowhere else round here that takes on farm lads. Nothing radical changing still means the same old risk of short weeks every bad winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and doing a good job so I'm not the first one cut. Leila and I would keep the food shop tight, own-brand everything. If the four-day weeks came back, I'd ask the haulage yard in town about weekend shifts loading lorries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. A bit of a worry in the back of my head every time I see a potato price on the radio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first when you're on four days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The electric, every time. They let you get behind a month or two before the letters get nasty. Last winter we were two months behind on the electric and Leila was in tears at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever look beyond Long Acre for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to. I like it there, I know the cattle, I know where everything is. Starting somewhere new and being the new lad again doesn't appeal.

say: I'd say **leave things** as they are.
I'd tell the pub I **never trusted** all that AI talk.
think: My real worry is **potato prices**, not AI.
A bad winter means **short weeks** again, with nowhere else to go.
do: Turn up and work hard so I'm **not the first cut**.
Keep the **food shop** to own-brand everything.
Ask the **haulage yard** about weekend loading if days drop.
feel: The same **background worry** as now, every time prices are on the radio.
S0.quote: Last winter we were two months behind on the electric and Leila was in tears at the kitchen table.
fieldNote: Karl's **existing pressure** is short weeks when potato prices fall.
He's **anxious even without AI**, because his income has already been cut once.
He resists change and dislikes the idea of **being the new lad** elsewhere.

steps.text: Keep turning up early at Long Acre to avoid being cut
Buy only own-brand food with Leila
Ask the haulage yard about weekend loading shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and buying and answering customers. That's Mr Dorran's office, not me. But Leila's supermarket, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible enough as long as it's not rushed. Some things will be better, some worse, and people need time. I'd not get worked up about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's Leila who gets hit first. The supermarket's already got self-checkouts, and if AI does the ordering and the customer bits, they'll want fewer people on the floor. My job's safe-ish for a while, but if Mr Dorran gets one of those camera graders for the potato store, my winter work goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and not rock the boat. Leila and I would stop the Sunday takeaway and the streaming thing. If the camera grader came in, I'd ask Mr Dorran to keep me on for the cattle full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, mainly for Leila, and a bit for my winters in the potato store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI. If the grader needed someone to run it, would you learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, wouldn't I, or he'd find someone who would. But I'd be slow at it and I'd hate it. I'm not a screens person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leila if her hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leila we'd manage, same as she told me last winter, then go and sit in the car for ten minutes on my own. Her mum and dad would help with food, they always do.

say: I'd say it's **sensible** as long as it's not rushed.
I'd say some things get better, some worse, and people need **time** to adjust.
I wouldn't get **worked up** about it in public.
think: **Leila's supermarket** gets hit first with AI ordering and self-checkouts.
A **camera grader** in the potato store would take my winter work.
do: Keep my head down and **not rock the boat**.
Stop the **Sunday takeaway** and the streaming subscription.
Ask Mr Dorran to keep me on **cattle full time** if the grader comes.
feel: A bit fearful for my **winters** in the potato store.
S1.quote: I'd tell Leila we'd manage, same as she told me last winter, then go and sit in the car for ten minutes on my own.
fieldNote: Karl sees **Leila's job** as more exposed to thinking AI than his own.
He'd learn new kit only **under pressure**, and reluctantly.
His family backstop is **Leila's parents**, who help with food.

steps.text: Keep his head down and work cattle and potatoes
Cancel the Sunday takeaway and the streaming subscription
Lean on Leila's parents for food if her hours drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots in 2031. That's mad. I'd be thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to slow it down and sort out what happens to ordinary people. Not stop it, maybe, but slow it. I'd say that at the pub and I'd vote for whoever said it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Long Acre gets a robot in 2031 and I'm finished there. The 2028 bit hits Leila's job first and Mr Dorran's paperwork, so we'd lose her money before mine. Then mine goes three years later, and I've got nothing else, I'm not trained for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything we don't need, straight away. I'd go and get my lorry licence, because Leila's dad drives for the haulage yard and says they're always short. And we'd probably have to move in with her parents for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground going soft under my boots. I don't like thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't robots drive lorries too by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah. I hadn't thought of that. Then I don't know what I'd do, I really don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have three years between the thinking AI and the robots. What would you do with them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and keep my head down, I suppose. I'm not the sort to go back to college at thirty, and Leila's the clever one, so she'd figure something out for both of us.

say: I'd say the government should **slow it down**, not stop it.
I'd say someone has to sort out what happens to **ordinary people**.
I'd **vote** for whoever said that plainly.
think: Leila's job goes in 2028, and mine with the **robots in 2031**.
I've got **no training** for anything else.
do: Get my **lorry licence** through Leila's dad.
Move in with **Leila's parents** for a while.
feel: Like the **ground going soft** under my boots.
S2.quote: I'm not the sort to go back to college at thirty, and Leila's the clever one, so she'd figure something out for both of us.
fieldNote: Karl expects **both household incomes** to go within three years.
His one plan, a **lorry licence**, collapses when he realises robots may drive too.
He'd hand the planning to **Leila**, a sign of his resistance and low confidence.

steps.text: Stop every non-essential direct debit this month
Book lorry licence training through Leila's dad
Move in with Leila's parents to save rent
Vote for candidates promising to slow AI down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. That's a bit better. More time to get used to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so the government and the bosses should plan it properly. I'd say farm lads shouldn't be the last ones anyone thinks about. That's about it, I'm not one for speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, eight years is a long way off for me. I'd probably worry about it in year six and do nothing before then. That's just how I am, I know it's not clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Long Acre and wait to see what Mr Dorran does. Maybe in a couple of years I'd ask the haulage yard about part-time driving. We'd keep things tight at home like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but further away. More like a cloud than a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably do nothing until year six. What would change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a robot actually working on a farm near us. If the Castle Hill farm got a robot and it worked, I'd sit up, but until then robots are just talk on the TV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Leila in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 still takes her supermarket job before mine. She'd probably retrain as a carer or something, she's good with people. We'd be all right if one of us kept working.

say: I'd say there's time, so **bosses and government** should plan it.
I'd say **farm lads** shouldn't be last in line.
think: Eight years feels **far away**, so I'd probably wait until year six.
I know waiting **isn't clever**, but that's how I am.
do: Keep working at **Long Acre** and watch what Mr Dorran does.
Ask the **haulage yard** about part-time driving in a couple of years.
feel: **Worried**, but more like a cloud than a storm.
S3.quote: If the Castle Hill farm got a robot and it worked, I'd sit up, but until then robots are just talk on the TV.
fieldNote: Karl openly admits he'd **wait and see**, knowing it isn't wise.
He'd only act after seeing a **robot** on a **nearby farm**.
He still expects **Leila's job** to go first, before his own.

steps.text: Wait until a robot appears on a nearby farm before acting
Keep working at Long Acre on four or five days
Keep the household food and bills budget tight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots in 2039. I'd be forty. That's a different man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's plenty of time to sort it out, so there's no excuse for anyone being left behind. I'd say people should start learning now. I probably wouldn't follow my own advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years feels like forever, so the robots wouldn't worry me much. What worries me is the next bad potato winter, and that's coming whatever happens with AI. Mr Dorran's sixty-four, and if his son takes over, who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, mostly. Maybe look at the lorry licence in a few years, slowly saving for it. Try to put a bit by each month with Leila, even twenty pounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not too bad about the robots. Still the usual worry about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Mr Dorran's son. What would change if he took over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His son, Ryan, did a farming degree and talks about drones and precision this and that. He'd change everything, probably fast. I'd be more worried about Mr Dorran's son taking over the farm than about AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do if Ryan took over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask him straight whether there's a place for me. If there isn't, I'd want to know early, not on a Friday afternoon. Then I'd go to the haulage yard.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for leaving people behind.
I'd tell people to **start learning** now, though I might not.
think: The robots feel **far off**, so they don't worry me much.
A bad **potato winter** worries me more, whatever AI does.
If Mr Dorran's son **Ryan** takes over, everything could change fast.
do: Carry on at Long Acre and **save slowly** for a lorry licence.
Put **twenty a month** aside with Leila.
S4.quote: I'd be more worried about Mr Dorran's son taking over the farm than about AGI.
fieldNote: With a decade, Karl's worry returns to **potato prices** and his boss's son.
He expects a **farm succession** to change his job before robots do.
He'd ask Ryan **early** whether he had a place, a sign of practical sense.

steps.text: Carry on at Long Acre through the next seasons
Save twenty pounds a month toward a lorry licence
Wait to see Ryan's plans before changing anything

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Leila and I would both lose our jobs within three years and we'd have nothing behind us. What would help is someone paying for me to learn something new, and a bit of money to live on while I do it, because I can't afford to stop working for a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we'd do if we lost the house. We rent, and the landlord wants the rent on the first of the month whatever's happening in the world. That's what keeps me up, not robots.

headlineQuote: The landlord wants the rent on the first of the month whatever's happening in the world.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old farm hand** at Long Acre, a beef and potato farm, living with his partner Leila.
He's already had his **days cut** once when potato prices fell, so he starts worried.
He **never uses AI** and would only learn new kit if forced.
He expects **Leila's supermarket job** to be hit before his own in most pictures.
With more warning time, he tends to **wait and see**, and admits it isn't wise.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both his and Leila's jobs gone within three years.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining** with a living allowance while he studies.
